newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish bourse seen returning to uptrend next week.
newsitem.headline: Polish bourse seen returning to uptrend next week.

text.p: The Warsaw bourse is expected to rise next week, returning to the recent uptrend after falls on Thursday and Friday, but some analysts saw a deeper profit-taking correction later in the year.

"It's likely the market will go up again, but the question is how far and how long it will rise", said Remigiusz Tarka of IB Austria Securitites, adding that the only negative signal he saw was possible high inflation in September.
But other analysts said that even a mediocre September inflation figure would beat last year's rise of three percent and keep inflation for the year below 20 percent.
Analysts said investors would be waiting for Friday's food price figure for September 11-20 to give them a clue on inflation for the whole month.
They said that after 1.4-percent food-price growth in the September 1-10 period the Polish central bank was unlikely to cut interest rates before mid-October.

Some analysts said the main WIG index could rise to about 16,000 points in the next few weeks but said that a deeper correction afterwards was possible due to the bourse's rise by over 90 percent since the beginning of the year.

"The economic and political climate is relatively stable, but the bourse is bound to suffer from profit-taking after the growth since the start of the year," said Ryszard Sikora, an analyst at Bank Slaski brokerage.
Some analysts said the downtrend could last two to three months, but said it was difficult to say where the market would find support.
The WIG rose 1.5 percent this week to 14,504.1 points from last Friday's close.
Analysts said the week's biggest loser Espebepe plunged 11.8 percent after it showed a consolidated loss of seven million zlotys in August.
Stalexport fell 11 percent for the week after a court refused it a tax refund of 75 million zlotys last week.
The main market's top gainers were BRE, which rose 17.3 percent, and Polfa Kutno, up 11.4 percent.
